The '''BMP-2''' ({{Langx|ru|Боевая Машина Пехоты|Boyevaya Mashina Pekhoty|combat machine/vehicle [of the] infantry}})<ref>{{cite web |url=http://milparade.com/Soderzhaniye.pdf |title=Soderzhaniye |trans-title=Table of Contents |format=PDF |website=Military Parade |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050511182011/http://milparade.com/Soderzhaniye.pdf |archive-date=11 May 2005 |url-status=dead}}</ref> is an amphibious [[infantry fighting vehicle]] introduced in the 1980s in the [[Soviet Union]], following on from the [[BMP-1]] of the 1960s.<ref name="urlBMP-2 | Weaponsystems.net">{{cite web |url=http://weaponsystems.net/weaponsystem/CC04%20-%20BMP-2.html |title=BMP-2 &#124; Weaponsystems.net |website=Weaponsystems.net |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181003043630/http://weaponsystems.net/weaponsystem/CC04%20-%20BMP-2.html |archive-date=3 October 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Development history ==
{{Main|BMP development}}
{{more citations needed|section|date=January 2016}}
[[File:Soviet BMP-1 IFV.JPEG|thumb|left|The [[BMP-1]], the predecessor to the BMP-2]]

Although the [[BMP-1]] was a revolutionary design, its main armament, the [[2A28 Grom]] and the 9S428 ATGM launcher capable of firing [[9M14 Malyutka]] (NATO: AT-3A Sagger A) and 9M14M Malyutka-M (NATO: AT-3B Sagger B) ATGMs, quickly became obsolete. Therefore, the Soviet Union decided to produce an updated and improved version of the BMP-1. The main emphasis was put on improving the main armament. In 1972, work got under-way to develop an improved version of the BMP-1.

During its combat debut in the [[Yom Kippur War|1973 Arab-Israeli War]], Egyptian and Syrian BMPs proved vulnerable to .50 calibre machine-gun fire in the sides and rear, and to 105&nbsp;mm [[M40 recoilless rifle]]s. The 2A28 Grom proved inaccurate beyond 500 metres, and the 9M14 Malyutka missile could not be guided effectively from the confines of the turret.

Several Soviet technical teams were sent to Syria in the wake of the war to gather information. These lessons, combined with observations of western AFV developments, resulted in a replacement project for the original BMP in 1974. The result was the BMP-1P upgrade, which was intended as a stopgap to address the most serious problems with the existing design.

Smoke grenade launchers were added to the rear of the turret and the [[MCLOS|manually guided]] 9M14 Malyutka missile system was replaced with the [[SACLOS|semi-automatically]] guided [[9K111 Fagot]] / [[9M113 Konkurs]] system. The BMP-1P was in production by the late 1970s. Existing BMP-1s were gradually upgraded to the BMP-1P standard during the 1980s.

== Design ==
{{More citations needed|section|date=January 2023}}
[[File:BMP21981graphic1.gif|thumb|right|BMP-2 graphic]]

The BMP-2 is broadly similar to the BMP-1. The most significant changes are:
* The commander now sits with the gunner in an enlarged, two-man turret.
* Armament changed to the 2A42 30&nbsp;mm autocannon and the 9P135M ATGM launcher capable of firing SACLOS guided [[9K111 Fagot|9M111 "Fagot"]] (AT-4 Spigot), [[9M113 Konkurs|9M113 "Konkurs"]] (AT-5 Spandrel) and 9M113M "Konkurs-M" (AT-5B Spandrel B) anti-tank missiles.
* Only seven troops can be carried instead of eight.
* Two rear infantry roof hatches instead of four.
* Slightly improved armour.

=== Layout ===
[[File:Курсанти Військової академії (м.Одеса) виконали практичне водіння бойових машин на плаву на морській ділянці узбережжя (27788951685).jpg|thumb|BMP-2 of the [[Armed Forces of Ukraine]] demonstrates its amphibious capabilities.]]
In the centre of the vehicle is the welded steel turret, which seats the commander and gunner, both of whom have hatches. The commander sits to the right and has three day-vision periscopes, a 1PZ-3 day-sight designed for anti-aircraft use with 1.2× and 4× magnification, an OU-3GA2 infra-red searchlight, a TNP-165A designator and a TKN-3B binocular sight with 4.75× day magnification and 4× night-sight magnification.

The gunner sits to the commander's left and has a smaller rectangular hatch with a rearward-facing day periscope. There are three other day periscopes facing forward and left. The gunner has a BPK-1-42 binocular sight with a moon/starlight vision range of 650 metres, or 350 metres using the infra-red searchlight, and a TNPT-1 designator. An FG-126 infra-red searchlight is mounted coaxially to the 30&nbsp;mm cannon.

The driver sits in the front left of the vehicle, with the engine in a separate compartment to his right. The driver has his own entry hatch above him, with three day-vision periscopes. The centre TNPO-170A periscope can be replaced with either a TNPO-350B extended periscope for amphibious operation or a TVNE-1PA [[night vision]] scope. An infantryman sits immediately behind the driver, and has a [[firing port]] and vision block. TNPO-170A periscopes are used throughout the vehicle and are electrically heated.

In the BMP-1 and BMP-2, ammunition is stored near or even inside the compartment{{Clarify|date=April 2025|reason=Which compartment?  Drivers, engine, troop? }}, which can lead to a catastrophic failure in case of a hull breach.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.n-tv.de/mediathek/videos/politik/Ukraine-jagt-Stachelschwein-Panzer-in-die-Luft-article25794624.html |title=Ukraine jagt "Stachelschwein"-Panzer in die Luft |trans-title=Ukraine blows up "porcupine" tank |website=n-tv.de |date=26 May 2025 |language=de |access-date=}}</ref>

[[File:The BMP's of the Indian Army roll out from an Indian Navy ship and travel through the sea for an amphibious assault during Exercise Tropex-09, at Madhavpur beach, Gujarat on February 09, 2009.jpg|thumb|[[Indian Army]] BMP-2's conducting simulated amphibious landings]]

=== Mobility ===
The BMP-1 and BMP-2 share the same chassis and have almost identical road performance. The BMP-2 is heavier, but also has a more powerful engine to compensate.

The BMP-2 is amphibious with little preparation, using hydrodynamic fairings to convert track momentum into water jets. Peacetime regulations require that any BMPs entering water must have a working radio set, since its bearings are not airtight and it can be carried away by currents in case of loss of engine power (the vehicle lacks an anchor).

=== Weapons ===
The main armament is a turret with a stabilized 30&nbsp;mm [[30 mm automatic cannon 2A42|2A42 autocannon]] with dual ammunition feeds, which provide a choice of 3UBR6 AP-T and 3UOR6 HE-T / 3UOF8 HE-I ammunition and 9M113 Konkurs ATGM. The gun has a selectable rate of fire, either slow at 200 to 300 rounds per minute or fast at 550 rounds per minute. This gives a continuous fire time of 100–150 seconds (or only 55 seconds, depending on the rate of fire chosen) before running out of ammunition. The original stabilization provides reasonable accuracy up to a speed of about 35 kilometres per hour.

The AP-T ammunition can penetrate 15 millimetres of armour at sixty degrees at 1,500 metres. A new APDS-T tungsten round can penetrate 25 millimetres at the same distance. A typical ammunition load is 160 rounds of AP ammunition and 340 rounds of HE ammunition. The ammunition sits in two trays located on the turret rear floor. The gun can be fired from either the commander's or the gunner's station.

The commander's 1PZ-3 sight is specifically designed for anti-aircraft operation. Combined with the high maximum elevation of 74 degrees, it allows the 30&nbsp;mm cannon to be used effectively against helicopters and slow flying aircraft. The turret traverse and elevation are powered and it can traverse 360 degrees in 10.28 seconds and elevate through 74 degrees in 12.33 seconds.

Reloading the BMP-2's 30&nbsp;mm cannon can be somewhat problematic and can take up to two hours, even if the ammunition is prepared. The cannon is normally only used on the slow rate of fire, otherwise, fumes from the weapon would build up in the turret faster than the extractor fan can remove them.{{Citation needed|date=December 2010}}

The effective range of the 30&nbsp;mm cannon is up to 1,500 metres against armour, 4,000 metres against ground targets, and 2,500 metres against air targets.

A coaxial [[PK machine gun|7.62&nbsp;mm PKT machine gun]] is mounted to the left of the 30&nbsp;mm cannon. 2,000 rounds of ammunition are carried for it. On the roof of the turret is an ATGM launcher. On Russian vehicles this fires 9M113 Konkurs missiles. On export models it normally fires 9K111 Fagot missiles. A ground-mount for the missile is carried, allowing it to be used away from the vehicle. The missiles are a substantial improvement on the 9M14 Malyutka missiles used on the BMP-1, in both range and accuracy.

Behind the turret is the troop compartment that holds six troops. A seventh sits just behind the driver. The troops sit back to back, along the center of the vehicle. Down each side of the compartment are three firing ports with periscopes. Access to the compartment is by the two rear doors, which hold fuel tanks. Both doors have integral periscopes. The left door has a firing port.

In addition to the main weapons, it can carry a [[MANPAD|man-portable surface-to-air missile launcher]] and two missiles, and an [[RPG-7|RPG launcher]] and five rounds. The vehicle is fitted with a PAZ [[Overpressure (CBRN protection)|overpressure NBC system]] and fire suppression system, and carries a GPK-59 [[gyrocompass]].

=== Countermeasures ===
The original BMP-1 had a vulnerability in its [[Anti-tank mine|mine]] protection scheme, which only became obvious during the war in Afghanistan. The one-man-turret fighting vehicle seated its driver and commander in tandem layout, in the front-left side of the hull alongside the diesel engine. When a BMP-1 hit a [[Tilt-rod fuze|tilt-rod]] anti-tank [[land mine]] its steeply sloped lower front glacis armour plate allowed the mine's arming rod to tilt with little resistance until the maximum deflection was reached, at which time the mine was already well under the chassis.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}}

When it subsequently detonated, the blast usually killed both the driver and the vehicle commander. This shortcoming was addressed in the BMP-2 design, where the tank commander shares the well-armoured two-man turret with the gunner. The driver's station has been enlarged and he is provided with an armored driver's seat, in addition to extra belly armor in the lower front.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}}

The IFV lacks the ability to install add-on protection packages like [[slat armor]] cages or [[explosive reactive armor]] (ERA).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://armyrecognition.com/weapons_defence_industry_military_technology_uk/russias_ministry_of_defense_to_overhaul_bmp-2_infanty_fighting_vehicles_52508162.html |title=Russia's Ministry of Defense to overhaul BMP-2 Infantry Fighting Vehicles |website=Army Recognition |date=25 August 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160828095326/http://www.armyrecognition.com/weapons_defence_industry_military_technology_uk/russias_ministry_of_defense_to_overhaul_bmp-2_infanty_fighting_vehicles_52508162.html |archive-date=28 August 2016 |url-status=dead |access-date=}}</ref> The BMP-2's armor is very similar to the original BMP-1, resistant to 23&nbsp;mm armor-piercing rounds on its frontal arc from 500 meters (and immune to 12.7&nbsp;mm armor-piercing from the same angle) and to 7.62x39 mm armor-piercing rounds to its sides. Its armor is slightly thinner than the BMP-1's but the higher-quality steel used in its construction grants it the same effective protection.

The basic hull armor on the BMP-2 can be easily penetrated by any shaped-charge missile, from the 66&nbsp;mm [[M72 LAW|LAW]] on up. One important modification carried out as the result of operational experience in Afghanistan was the fitting of a second layer of stand-off armor, usually a high resistant ballistic rubber-like material, to act as [[spaced armour]] around the top of the hull sides and around the turret.

According to Russian sources, the vehicles repaired as of November 2023 are equipped with attachments to install additional protection kits.<ref>{{cite web | title=ЦАМТО / / В российскую армию передана партия отремонтированных БМП-2 | website=ЦАМТО / Центр анализа мировой торговли оружием | date=2023-11-22 | url=https://armstrade.org/includes/periodics/news/2023/1122/094576534/detail.shtml | language=ru | ref={{sfnref | ЦАМТО / Центр анализа мировой торговли оружием | 2023}} | access-date=2023-11-23}}</ref>

== Service history ==
[[File:Yudh Abhyas-09 BMP.JPG|thumb|The [[Indian Army]]'s upgraded BMP-2 ''Sarath'' during military exercise in [[Rajasthan]], India]]
In the Soviet Army, BMPs were typically issued to the motor rifle battalions of tank regiments. In a typical motor-rifle division, one motor-rifle regiment had BMPs, the other two had wheeled [[BTR-60|BTRs]].

Proliferation varied greatly among the rest of the Warsaw Pact nations. For example, at least some East German motor-rifle divisions were recorded to have all three motor-rifle regiments with BMPs, ranging down to the Romanian and Bulgarian Armies, some of whose divisions had no BMPs at all.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.orbat.com/site/history/historical/nato/warsawpact.html |title=Warsaw Pact |website=Orbat.com |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303230623/http://www.orbat.com/site/history/historical/nato/warsawpact.html |archive-date=3 March 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

Poland planned to replace its [[BMP-1#Poland|BWP-1]] with [[BMP-2#Poland|BWP-2]] (BMP-2 and BMP-2D); but, because of financial problems, only ordered 62 vehicles in 1988, which were delivered in 1989. Since obtaining a sufficient number of BWP-2 vehicles after the political changes of 1989 became impossible, Poland was forced to abandon this plan. The 62 BWP-2 that Poland bought were sold to Angola in 1995. However, after shipping 42 of the IFVs and receiving a partial payment of 6.3 million USD, Angola withdrew from the deal, refusing to take the remaining 20 vehicles. These 20 additional vehicles were later sold to Togo and left Poland in 1997.<ref name="Pancerni.net 1">{{cite web |url=http://www.pancerni.abajt.pl/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=71&Itemid=83 |title=BMP-2 |website=Pancerni.net |language=pl |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070818081435/http://www.pancerni.abajt.pl/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=71&Itemid=83 |archive-date=18 August 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="SIPRI" />

== Variants ==
[[File:BMP-2D IFV.jpg|thumb|right|BMP-2D on display near the Great Patriotic War Museum, Kyiv, 4 September 2005]]

=== Soviet Union and Russian Federation ===
[[File:BMP-2M.jpg|thumb|right|BMP-2M "Berezhok"]]
* '''BMP-2 obr. 1980''' – Initial production model.<ref name="urlBMP-2 IFV tracked armored Infantry Fighting Vehicle video | Russia Russian army light armoured vehicle UK | Russia Russian army military equipment vehicles UK">{{cite web |url=https://www.armyrecognition.com/russia_russian_army_light_armoured_vehicle_uk/bmp-2_ifv_tracked_armoured_infantry_fighting_vehicle_data_sheet_specifications_pictures_video.html |title=BMP-2 IFV tracked armored Infantry Fighting Vehicle video &#124; Russia Russian army light armoured vehicle UK &#124; Russia Russian army military equipment vehicles UK |website=Armyrecognition.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181105015420/https://www.armyrecognition.com/russia_russian_army_light_armoured_vehicle_uk/bmp-2_ifv_tracked_armoured_infantry_fighting_vehicle_data_sheet_specifications_pictures_video.html |archive-date=5 November 2018 |url-status=live |author1=Administrator }}</ref>
** '''BMP-2 obr. 1984''' – Improved version with "kovriki" armour on turret front.
*** '''BMP-2 obr. 1986''' – Late-production model with new BPK-2-42 sight instead of the BPK-1-42.
** '''BMP-2D''' (D stands for ''dorabotanaya'' – modified) – Fitted with additional spaced type steel [[appliqué armour]] on the hull sides, under the driver's and commander's stations, and 6&nbsp;mm thick appliqué armour on the turret. Owing to the added weight, the vehicle is no longer amphibious. It also has provision for mounting a mine clearing system under the nose of the vehicle. In service since 1982, it saw service during [[Soviet–Afghan War]]. During that conflict, western observers saw the vehicle for the first time and gave it a designation '''BMP-2E'''.{{Citation needed|date=September 2019}}
** '''BMP-2K''' (K stands for ''komandirskaya'' – command) – Command variant fitted with two whip antennas mounted on the rear of the hull, one behind the turret and one on the right-hand side of the rear of the vehicle, one IFF antenna (pin stick) on the left-hand side of the rear of the vehicle and a support for a telescopic mast in the front of the IFF antenna. The firing port equipped with the periscope was removed from either side of the vehicle. The antennae on the turret was removed. The radio equipment consists either of the R-123M and R-130M radio sets, or the more modern R-173, R-126 and R-10. The crew consists of six men.{{Citation needed|date=September 2019}}
** '''BMP-2M''' – This is the general designator for upgraded (''modernizirovannyj'') versions.
*** The upgrade package from 2008<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.janes.com/products/janes/defence-security-report.aspx?id=1065927428 |title=Defence Security Report |website=Janes.com |date=8 December 2008 |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120916123637/http://www.janes.com/products/janes/defence-security-report.aspx?id=1065927428 |archive-date=16 September 2012 |url-status=dead}}</ref> consists of the UTD-23 400&nbsp;hp (294&nbsp;kW) turbocharged engine, BPK-3-42 gunner`s sight and TKN-AI commander`s sight, additional passive armour, an [[AGS-17|AG-17 "Plamya"]] grenade launcher and a KBM-2 air conditioning unit. Furthermore, the upgraded vehicle will have an improved suspension with road wheels of higher load carrying capacity, enhanced-hardness torsion bars, power-consuming shock absorbers and tracks with rubber pad shoes.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kurganmash.ru/en/machines/bmp2u/fire_power/ |title=Fire power |website=Kurganmash.ru |publisher=Kurganmashzavod |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110803103731/http://www.kurganmash.ru/en/machines/bmp2u/fire_power/ |archive-date=3 August 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
*** '''BMP-2M "Berezhok"'''<ref>{{cite web |url=http://armstass.su/?page=article&aid=28887&cid=103 |title=Армс-Тасс |trans-title=Arms-Tass |language=ru |website=Armstass.su |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111002122952/http://armstass.su/?page=article&aid=28887&cid=103 |archive-date=2 October 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref> – Modernized version from [[KBP Instrument Design Bureau|KBP]]. This version has B05Ya01 Berezhok turret equipped with 2A42 30mm autocannon, PKMT 7.62mm coaxial machine gun, [[AGS-30]] grenade launcher, 2+2 launchers for ATGM [[9M133M Kornet-M|9M133M "Kornet-M"]] and new day/night sights SOZh-TM (as found on BMP-3). Hull is fitted with armored side skirts and slat (cage) armor. There is an improved UTD-23 diesel engine (400&nbsp;hp) coupled with automatic transmission. Suspension is also improved. This upgrade was selected by Algeria,<ref>Military Parade 2006-6-page 61</ref> and Russia will upgrade several hundred of its vehicles.<ref name="ArmyRec_Berezhok_2017">{{cite web |url=https://www.armyrecognition.com/october_2017_global_defense_security_news_industry/russian_bmp-2_and_bmd-2_upgraded_with_new_berezhok_weapon_station.html |title=Russian BMP-2 and BMD-2 upgraded with new Berezhok weapon station |website=Army Recognition |date=3 October 2017 |access-date=10 September 2023 Siberia received first BMP-2M IFV armed with Berezhok combat module |website=Army Recognition |date=21 June 2018 |access-date=21 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180621221146/http://www.armyrecognition.com/june_2018_global_defense_security_army_news_industry/russian_army_in_siberia_received_first_bmp-2m_ifv_armed_with_berezhok_combat_module.html |archive-date=21 June 2018 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.armyrecognition.com/army-2018_news_russia_online_show_daily/army_2018_uralvagonzavod_uvz_will_repair_230_bmp-2_ifvs_before_2020_under_a_contract_with_the_russian_defense_ministry.html |title=Army 2018: UralVagonZavod UVZ will repair 230 BMP-2 IFVs before 2020 under a contract with the Russian Defense Ministry |website=Army Recognition |access-date=28 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180829073554/https://www.armyrecognition.com/army-2018_news_russia_online_show_daily/army_2018_uralvagonzavod_uvz_will_repair_230_bmp-2_ifvs_before_2020_under_a_contract_with_the_russian_defense_ministry.html |archive-date=29 August 2018 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://armstrade.org/includes/periodics/mainnews/2022/0817/084269022/detail.shtml | title=ЦАМТО / Главное / На форуме «Армия-2022» подписаны 7 и вручены 29 госконтрактов с 26 предприятиями ОПК }}</ref>
** '''BMO-1''' (''boyevaya mashina ognemyotchikov'') – Transport vehicle for a flamethrower squad armed with 30 [[RPO-A Shmel|RPO-A "Shmel"]] 93&nbsp;mm thermobaric rocket launchers. It is equipped with storage racks and a dummy turret. The crew consists of seven soldiers. It entered service in 2001.{{Citation needed|date=September 2019}}

=== Former Czechoslovakia ===
* '''BVP-2''' (''bojové vozidlo pěchoty'') – Czechoslovak-produced version of BMP-2.
* '''BVP-2V''' or '''VR 1p''' (''vozidlo velitele roty'') – Company commander's vehicle with tent, telescopic mast and radiosets RF 1325 (x 2), IPRS 32, RF 1301 and NS 2480D.<ref name="Valka_BVP-2V">{{cite web |url=http://forum.valka.cz/viewtopic.php?p=105568 |title=CZE – BVP-2V (velitelské stanoviště) |trans-title=CZE – BVP-2V (command post) |website=Valka.cz |access-date=20 September 2011 |language=cs}}</ref><ref name="BRDM2_BVP-2V">{{cite web |url=http://www.brdm2.estranky.cz/fotoalbum/pasova-obrnena-vozidla-a-jejich-varianty/Velitelske-stanoviste-BVP-2V |title=Velitelské stanoviště BVP-2V |trans-title=Command post BVP-2V |website=brdm2.estranky.cz |access-date=20 September 2011 |language=cs}}</ref>
* '''VPV''' (VPV stands for ''vyprošťovací pásové vozidlo'') – BVP-2 conversion into an ARV developed at the ZTS Martin Research and Development Institute and production commenced at the ZTS Martin plant (which is now in Slovakia) in 1984. It is equipped with a powered crane with 5 tonnes capacity, heavy winch, wider troop compartment etc. Hatches on top of the turret and the troop compartment were removed. The vehicle is divided into four compartments: engine, commander's, driver's and repair/cargo. The crew consists of a commander/crane operator, driver/welder/slinger and a logistician/mechanic. The vehicle is armed with a pintle-mounted 7.62&nbsp;mm PKT light machine gun. A small number of those vehicles was also based on BVP-1.<ref name="BRDM2_VPV">{{cite web |url=http://www.brdm2.estranky.cz/fotoalbum/pasova-obrnena-vozidla-a-jejich-varianty/Vyprostovaci-pasove-vozidlo---VPV |title=Vyprošťovací pásové vozidlo – VPV |trans-title=Tracked recovery vehicle – VPV |website=brdm2.estranky.cz |language=cs |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080308044139/http://www.brdm2.estranky.cz/fotoalbum/pasova-obrnena-vozidla-a-jejich-varianty/Vyprostovaci-pasove-vozidlo---VPV |archive-date=8 March 2008 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== India ===
[[File:Indian Army BMP-2.jpg|right|thumb|An Indian BMP-2 "Sarath" on display]]

* '''BMP-2 "Sarath"''' ("[[Ratha|Chariot]] of Victory"), also known as '''BMP-II''' – Indian licence-produced variant of the BMP-2,<ref name="ofb">{{cite web |url=http://ofbindia.gov.in/products/data/armoured/4.htm |title=Ordnance Factory Board |website=ofbindia.gov.in |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110621161821/http://ofbindia.gov.in/products/data/armoured/4.htm |archive-date=21 June 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref> built by [[Ordnance Factory Medak]] since 1987.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Update: Indian Army to get 156 additional BMP-2 ICVs |url=https://www.janes.com/defence-news/news-detail/aba17155-3c80-4297-98c5-3f93128cb0e0 |access-date=2024-06-01 |website=Janes.com |language=en}}</ref> The turret is equipped with an [[Anti-tank guided missile|ATGM]] launcher while each vehicle can carry 4 missiles.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-12-03 |title=Indian Army and Anti-Tank Guided Missile |url=https://www.strategicfront.org/forums/threads/indian-army-and-anti-tank-guided-missile.102/ |access-date=2024-08-19 |website=Strategic Front Forum – Indian Defence and Strategic Forum |language=en-US}}</ref>Some units have also [[Kanchan armour]] and [[Slat armor|slat armour]] modifications.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MSN |url=https://www.msn.com/en-in/news/india/indian-army-battle-axe-division-conducts-integrated-firing-drills-in-rajasthan-s-desert/ar-AA1WvjHZ?ocid=msedgntp&pc=U531&cvid=69946a5ffd0e47779ae50ecc6bdde9be&ei=107 |access-date=2026-02-17 |website=www.msn.com}}</ref> 
** The first vehicle, assembled from components supplied by KBP, was ready in 1987. By 1999, about 90% of the complete vehicle and its associated systems were being produced in India. It was estimated that, by 2007, 1,250 vehicles had been built. As of February 2020, around 2,500 Saraths were made.<ref name="armyrecognition.com">{{Cite web|url=https://www.armyrecognition.com/february_2020_global_defense_security_army_news_industry/india_manufactured_around_2500_bmp-2_ifv_under_russian_license.html|title=India manufactured around 2,500 BMP-2 IFVs under Russian license|website=armyrecognition.com|date=7 February 2020 }}</ref>
**On June 2, 2020, India's Ministry of Defence announced placement of an order of 156 BMP-2 Sarath vehicles (Infantry Combat Vehicles) for the [[Indian Army]]'s infantry units.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://psuwatch.com/ofb-supply-156-upgraded-bmp-infantry-combat-vehicles/|title=OFB gets supply order of 156 BMP Infantry Combat Vehicles worth Rs 1,094 Cr |date=2 June 2020 |website=PSUWATCH |access-date=17 January 2023|last=Defence Watch Bureau}}</ref>  The {{INRConvert|1093|c|year=2020}} order will be executed by state owned [[Ordnance Factory Board]], and BMP-2/2K Sarath will be produced by [[Ordnance Factory Medak]]. The delivery is expected to be complete by 2023.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-03-14 |title=MoD inks contract with AVNL to upgrade Infantry Combat Vehicle BMP2 to BMP2M |url=https://www.financialexpress.com/business/defence-mod-inks-contract-with-avnl-to-upgrade-infantry-combat-vehicle-bmp2-to-bmp2m-3425280/ |access-date=2024-05-07 |website=Financialexpress |language=en}}</ref>
**On 5 August 2025, the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) accorded the Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) for the procurement of new thermal imager-based driver night-sights for the Indian Army's BMP-II fleet.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-08-06 |title=MoD clears big arms deals, including BrahMos, armed drones, worth Rs 67,000cr |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/mod-clears-big-arms-deals-including-brahmos-armed-drones-worth-rs-67000cr/articleshow/123127687.cms |access-date=2025-08-06 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}}</ref><ref>{{Cite press release |title=DAC clears proposals worth Rs 67,000 crore to enhance operational capability of the Armed Forces |date=2025-08-05 |publisher=[[Press Information Bureau]] |url=https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2152742 |access-date=2025-08-06}}</ref>

India has also developed the following versions of the "Sarath":
*'''BMP-2 [[Light tank|Light Tank]]''' – DRDO developed light tank on BMP-2 Chassis [[DRDO light tank]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Singh |first1=Ajay |title=The Search for A Light Tank |url=https://forceindia.net/guest-column/search-light-tank/ |access-date=29 September 2023 |magazine=FORCE}}</ref>
*'''BMP-2K "Sarath" Carrier Command Post Tracked''' – Command vehicle, similar to the Soviet/Russian version.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Technologies and Products {{!}} Defence Research and Development Organisation – DRDO, Ministry of Defence, Government of India|url=https://www.drdo.gov.in/technology-cluster-links/labs-products-detail/1265/175|access-date=2021-10-14|website=drdo.gov.in}}</ref>
*'''BMP-2M''' – Upgraded BMP-2 shown in [[Defence Exhibition Organisation#DefExpo|DEFEXPO 2022]] with a [[loitering munition]] system (LMS), anti-tank guided missiles and an armament upgrade with an integrated [[fire-control system]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Defexpo 2022: India unveils upgraded BMPs |url=https://www.janes.com/defence-news/news-detail/defexpo-2022-india-unveils-upgraded-bmps |access-date=2024-03-14 |website=Janes.com |language=en}}</ref> The upgrades include with TISAS (Thermal Imaging Stand Alone Sights), better fire control, two [[Thermobaric weapon|thermobaric]] missiles and two tandem warhead [[9M113 Konkurs|Konkurs]] missiles. It also has an integrated TI sight, a [[Laser rangefinder|Laser Range Finder]] (LRF), and has an [[Automatic grenade launcher|Automatic Grenade Launcher]] (AGL) mounted on the turret which is also stabilised in the horizontal plane. Indian Army will upgrade the older variants to BMP-2M variant at an initial rate of 100 units per year. Later the rate will be increased to 125 per year.<ref name="Indian Army: Armoured Fighting Vehicles">{{cite web |date=20 February 2002 |title=Land Forces Site – BMP-2 |url=http://www.bharat-rakshak.com/LAND-FORCES/Equipment/Armour/346-BMP-2.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121007005545/http://www.bharat-rakshak.com/LAND-FORCES/Equipment/Armour/346-BMP-2.html |archive-date=7 October 2012 |access-date=2012-04-21 |publisher=Bharat Rakshak}}</ref> On 14 March 2024, [[Ministry of Defence (India)|Ministry of Defence]] signed an initial contract with [[Armoured Vehicles Nigam|Armoured Vehicle Nigam Limited]] to upgrade 693 units to BMP-2M configuration.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MoD inks contract with AVNL for 693 Armament Upgrades of Infantry Combat Vehicle BMP2 to BMP2M |url=https://pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=2014345 |access-date=2024-03-15 |website=pib.gov.in}}</ref>
*'''[[DRDO Armoured Ambulance|Armoured Ambulance]]''' – This version retains the turret but without the gun or smoke grenade launchers. The troop compartment has been modified to carry four stretchers.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Technologies and Products {{!}} Defence Research and Development Organisation – DRDO, Ministry of Defence, Government of India|url=https://www.drdo.gov.in/technology-cluster-links/labs-products-detail/1261/175|access-date=2021-10-14|website=drdo.gov.in}}</ref>
*'''Armoured Vehicle Tracked Light Repair''' – Armoured recovery vehicle, fitted with a light hydraulic crane.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Light Repair [www.bharat-rakshak.com]|url=https://www.bharat-rakshak.com/ARMY/Galleries/Mod/ICVEHICLES/BMP1/0364.jpg.html|access-date=2021-10-14|website=bharat-rakshak.com|archive-date=28 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028165931/https://www.bharat-rakshak.com/ARMY/Galleries/Mod/ICVEHICLES/BMP1/0364.jpg.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
*'''Armoured Amphibious Dozer''' (AAD) – Turret-less combat engineer vehicle, fitted with a folding dozer blade at the rear, mine ploughs, a main winch with a capacity of 8,000&nbsp;kg and a rocket-propelled earth anchor for self-recovery.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Armoured Amphibious Dozer {{!}} Defence Research and Development Organisation – DRDO, Ministry of Defence, Government of India|url=https://www.drdo.gov.in/armoured-amphibious-dozer|access-date=2021-10-14|website=drdo.gov.in}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Armoured Amphibious Dozer. DRDO|url=https://tanknutdave.com/the-indian-armoured-amphibious-dozer/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140507045205/http://tanknutdave.com/the-indian-armoured-amphibious-dozer/|archive-date=7 May 2014|access-date=14 October 2021}}</ref>
*'''[[Armoured Engineer Reconnaissance Vehicle]]''' (AERV) – This version has no gun and is fitted with specialised equipment, including an echo-sounder, a water current metre, a laser range finder and GPS. On the left rear of the hull, a marking system with 40 rods is fitted.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Armoured Engineer Reconnaissance Vehicle (AERV) {{!}} Defence Research and Development Organisation – DRDO, Ministry of Defence, Government of India |url=https://www.drdo.gov.in/armoured-engineer-reconnaissance-vehicle-aerv |access-date=2021-10-14 |website=drdo.gov.in}}</ref>
* '''[[Weapon of mass destruction|NBC]] [[Reconnaissance vehicle|Reconnaissance Vehicle]]''' (NBCRV) – For detection of nuclear, biological and chemical contamination. The NBCRV was developed by [[Defence Research and Development Organisation|DRDO]] and VRDE and has been ordered by the Indian army.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NBC Reconnaissance Vehicle Mk-I {{!}} Defence Research and Development Organisation – DRDO, Ministry of Defence, Government of India |url=https://www.drdo.gov.in/nbc-reconnaissance-vehicle-mk-i |access-date=2021-10-14 |website=drdo.gov.in}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=NBC-Recce Vehicle (NBC-RV) MK-I {{!}} Defence Research and Development Organisation – DRDO, Ministry of Defence, Government of India |url=https://www.drdo.gov.in/nbc-recce-vehicle-nbc-rv-mk-i |access-date=2021-10-14 |website=drdo.gov.in}}</ref>
* '''Carrier Mortar Tracked Vehicle''' – This turret-less version has an 81&nbsp;mm mortar mounted in the modified troop compartment. The mortar is fired through an opening in the hull roof that has two hinged doors. It has a max. range of 5,000&nbsp;m and a normal rate of fire of 6–8 rds/min. There is also a longe-range version of the mortar.<ref name="ofb_weapons">{{cite web |url=http://ofbindia.gov.in/products/data/weapons/wme/4.htm |title=Ordnance Factory Board – Weapons |website=ofbindia.gov.in |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071130001104/http://ofbindia.gov.in/products/data/weapons/wme/4.htm |archive-date=30 November 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The vehicle carries 108 mortar rounds and is also fitted with a 7.62&nbsp;mm machine gun with 2,350 rounds. Crew: 2+4. The first prototype was completed in 1997.<ref name="ofb_armoured_5">{{cite web |url=http://ofbindia.gov.in/products/data/armoured/5.htm |title=Ordnance Factory Board – Armoured Vehicles |website=ofbindia.gov.in |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071130000912/http://ofbindia.gov.in/products/data/armoured/5.htm |archive-date=30 November 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
* '''[[Nag (missile)#NAMICA|NAMICA]]''' (''Nag Missile Carrier'') – part of the [[Nag (missile)|Nag ATGM]]. The Nag missile is launched from a retractable armoured launcher that contains six launch tubes and the guidance package. "Nag" is a fire-and-forget top-attack [[ATGM]] with a tandem-HEAT warhead and a range of at least 4&nbsp;km.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-08-20 |title=NAG Missile Carrier NAMICA-2 To Dramatically Boost Indian Army's Firepower Against China |url=https://eurasiantimes.com/nag-missile-carrier-namica-2-to-dramatically-boost-indian-armys-firepower-against-china/ |access-date=2021-10-14 |website=Latest Asian, Middle-East, EurAsian, Indian News |language=en-US}}</ref>
* '''[[Akash (missile)|Akash]]''' – Air-defence missile system that is based on a modified "Sarath" chassis with 7 road wheels. On top of the hull there's a launcher for three SAMs with a range of 27&nbsp;km and semi-active homing guidance.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Chopra |first=Anil |date=2021-02-07 |title=Akash Air Defence Missile– India's Formidable Weapon System |url=https://airpowerasia.com/2021/02/07/akash-air-defence-missile-indias-formidable-weapon-system/ |access-date=2021-10-14 |website=Air Power Asia |language=en}}</ref>
*'''Trishul Combat Vehicle''' – A variant with four [[Trishul (missile)|Trishul]] SAM launchers and a [[Flycatcher (radar)|Flycatcher]] radar system.{{sfn|Cullen|Foss|1992|page=113}} The vehicle entered trials in 2001, but never entered service.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kumar |first1=Neha |title=DRDO's Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme {{!}} IPCS |url=http://www.ipcs.org/focusthemsel.php?articleNo=2480 |access-date=29 September 2023 |website=Institute of Peace and Conflict Studies}}</ref>
* '''[[Rajendra Radar|Rajendra]]''' – This is a multifunctional 3-D phased radar ('''MUFAR'''), associated with the "Akash" system. It is also based on the stretched chassis.<ref name=":0" />
* '''BMP-2 UGV "[[Muntra]]"''' – is a family of unmanned reconnaissance vehicles developed by [[DRDO]], The Muntra family has several versions such as "S" version is fitted with equipment used to detect nuclear, biological and chemical contamination while the "M" version is designed to detect mines and "N" for operations in Nuclear and chemical contaminated areas.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2017-07-29 |title=DRDO develops India's first unmanned tank, Muntra; rolls it out of Chennai lab |url=http://www.firstpost.com/india/drdo-develops-indias-first-unmanned-tank-muntra-rolls-it-out-of-chennai-lab-3870693.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170811070723/http://www.firstpost.com/india/drdo-develops-indias-first-unmanned-tank-muntra-rolls-it-out-of-chennai-lab-3870693.html |archive-date=11 August 2017 |access-date=2017-08-11 |work=Firstpost.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Combat Vehicles Research & Development Estt (CVRDE) Chennai – CVRDE Chennai – DRDO DRDO |url=https://www.drdo.gov.in/drdo/labs1/CVRDE/English/indexnew.jsp?pg=products.jsp |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170811055308/https://www.drdo.gov.in/drdo/labs1/CVRDE/English/indexnew.jsp?pg=products.jsp |archive-date=11 August 2017 |access-date=2017-08-11 |website=Drdo.gov.in}}</ref>
* '''[[OFB 105 mm SPG|105&nbsp;mm Self-Propelled Gun]]''' – This is OFB's mechanized version of the Indian [[Indian Field Gun|Indian Light Field Gun]] (EQPT 105/37 LFG E2) with 42 rounds stowed. The gun is mounted in a lightly armoured turret.<ref name="Flickr_OFB_105_Specs">{{cite web |url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/47686239@N03/4370232436/ |title=OFB 105 mm SPG Specs |website=[[Flickr]] |date=19 February 2010 |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160203174622/https://www.flickr.com/photos/47686239@N03/4370232436/ |archive-date=3 February 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Flickr_OFB_105_BMP2">{{cite web |url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/47686239@N03/4369483629/ |title=OFB 105 mm Tracked SPG on BMP II |website=[[Flickr]] |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160203174622/https://www.flickr.com/photos/47686239@N03/4369483629/ |archive-date=3 February 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref> The 105&nbsp;mm SPG was shown for the first time in public in February 2010 during DEFEXPO-2010 in New Delhi and was planned to replace the [[FV433 Abbot SPG]] in the Indian army,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Choudhari |first1=Palash |last2=Karthikeyan |first2=Varun |last3=Madhavan |first3=Anoop |title=Military Balance India Vs China Part-3 Indian artillery systems |url=http://fullafterburner.weebly.com/next-gen-weapons/military-balance-india-vs-china-part-3-indian-artillery-systems |access-date=29 September 2023 |website=Full Afterburner |language=en}}</ref> but it wasn't accepted into service.

=== Israel ===
* '''BMP-2''' upgrade designed by Nimda fitting it with new power unit and automatic transmission which improves both mobility and reliability.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nimda.co.il/projects2.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090302085251/http://www.nimda.co.il/projects2.html|url-status=dead|title=Nimda Group Ltd. – commercial and military systems in energy, transportation and automotive applications|archive-date=2 March 2009}}</ref>

=== Poland ===
* '''BWP-2''' – The Polish designation for the BMP-2 and BMP-2D, which stands for "Bojowy Wóz Piechoty".{{Citation needed|date=September 2019}}

=== Finland ===
[[File:Lippujuhlan päivän 2017 paraati 080 BMP-2M Ps 153-74.JPG|right|thumb|Finnish BMP-2MD]]
* '''BMP-2MD''' – Finnish modernisation of the BMP-2, which includes thermal camouflage, thermal sights, anti-aircraft sight and new day/night optics for the gunner and commander, heated cabin and seats, new external storage boxes functioning also as spaced armour and new radio and communications systems.<ref>{{cite web|title=Suomi modernisoi noin 100 rynnäkköpanssarivaunua – tarkoitus sinnitellä ainakin 2030-luvulle asti|url=http://www.hs.fi/kotimaa/art-2000002796705.html|publisher=[[Helsingin Sanomat]]|date=30 January 2015|access-date=20 July 2017|language=fi|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170916010941/http://www.hs.fi/kotimaa/art-2000002796705.html|archive-date=16 September 2017|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Rynnäkköpanssarivaunu BMP-2 MD|url=http://maavoimat.fi/bmp2|publisher=[[Finnish Defence Forces]]|access-date=20 July 2017|language=fi|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170627064058/http://maavoimat.fi/bmp2|archive-date=27 June 2017|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Operators ==
=== Current operators ===
<!--READ FIRST: This section is for cited entries only. Please do not add entries into this list without a citation from a reliable source. All entries without a citation will be removed. Thank you.-->

* {{ALG}} – 225 along with 2,250 9M111 Fagot ATGMs were ordered in 1989 from the Soviet Union and delivered between 1990 and 1991. 54 BVP-2s and BVP-2Ks were ordered in 1994 from Slovakia and delivered between 1995 and 1996. 64 were ordered in 1998 from Ukraine and delivered between 1998 and 1999 (the vehicles were previously in Soviet and later Ukrainian service).<ref name="SIPRI" /> Estimated to have 220 BMP-2 and 760 BMP-2M in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=315}} 
* {{ANG}} – 65, along with 650 9M111 Fagot ATGMs, were ordered in 1987 from the Soviet Union and delivered in 1987. 7 were ordered in 1993 from Hungary and delivered in 1993 (the vehicles were previously in Hungarian service and were sold via Czech Republic). 42 BMP-2s were ordered in 1994 from Poland and delivered between 1994 and 1995 (the vehicles were previously in Polish service). 65 were ordered in 1997 from Russia and delivered in 1998 (the vehicles were possibly previously in Soviet and later Russian service). 62 were ordered in 1999 from Belarus and delivered in 1999 (the vehicles were previously in Soviet and later Belarusian service). 31 were ordered in 1999 from Ukraine and delivered in 1999 (the vehicles were previously in Soviet and later Ukrainian service).<ref name="SIPRI" /> 250 BMP-1 and BMP-2 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=433}}
* {{ARM}} – 15 as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=171}}
[[File:BVP-2 military parade Prague.jpg|thumb|right|Czech BVP-2 on a Military parade in Prague, 28 October 2008.]] [[File:Two Fninish BMP-2s.JPG|thumb|right|Two Finnish BMP-2s, 25 October 2004]]
* {{AZE}} – 101 in service with the army and 168 BMP-1 and BMP-2 in service with the [[State Border Service of Azerbaijan|State Border Service]] as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=172−174}}
* {{BLR}} – 906 as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=175}}
* {{CZE}} – 120 in service as of 2025.<ref name="IISS2022_p2613" /> 200 inherited from former Czechoslovakia.<ref name="Pancerni.net 1" /> 
* {{FIN}} – 110 BMP-2MD in service as of 2025.<ref name="IISS2022_p2613">[[International Institute for Strategic Studies]]: The Military Balance 2025</ref> 20 were ordered in 1988 from the Soviet Union and delivered between 1988 and 1989. Further 84 were ordered in 1991 from the Soviet Union and delivered in 1992 by Russia.<ref name="SIPRI"/> 
* {{GEO}} – 40 were ordered in 2004 from Ukraine and were delivered between 2004 and 2005 (the vehicles were previously in Soviet and later Ukrainian service).<ref name="SIPRI" /> 89 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=177}}
* {{IND}}<ref name="Pancerni.net 1" /> – 700 BMP-2 "Sarath" ordered in 1984 from the Soviet Union and delivered between 1987 and 1991 (most produced in India). 400 BMP-2 "Sarath" ordered in 1985 and produced in India between 1992 and 1995 at [[Ordnance Factory Medak]] of [[Ordnance Factories Board]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ofbindia.gov.in/products/data/armoured/4.htm |title=Ordnance Factory Board |website=Ofbindia.gov.in |access-date=2013-11-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110621161821/http://ofbindia.gov.in/products/data/armoured/4.htm |archive-date=21 June 2011 |url-status=live}}</ref> under Russian licence. 123 BMP-2K ordered in 2006 from Russia and delivered between 2007 and 2008.<ref name="SIPRI" /> 2,400 BMP-2 Sarath, plus an unknown number of BMP-2K and [[armoured engineering vehicle]]s in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=247−248}} 
* {{flag|Kurdistan Region}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=IRGC Equipped BMP-2 with Unmanned Turret |date=13 February 2022 |website=TurDef |url=https://turdef.com/article/irgc-equipped-bmp-2-with-unmanned-turret}}</ref>
* {{IRN}} – 1,500 ordered in 1991 from Russia and 413 were delivered between 1993 and 2001 of which 82 were delivered directly by Russia and 331 were assembled in Iran.<ref name="SIPRI" /> 400 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=324}}
* {{INA}} – 9 ordered in 1998 from Ukraine and delivered in 1998 (the vehicles were possibly previously in Soviet and later Ukrainian service and were sold via Slovakia). 2 more ordered the same year (sold via Slovakia. 11 BVP-2s ordered in 1999 from Slovakia and delivered in 2000 (the vehicles were probably previously in Czechoslovak and later Slovak service).<ref name="SIPRI" /> 22 ex-Czech BVP-2s are currently in service in the [[Indonesian Marine Corps|Marine Corps]] as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=253−256}}
* {{CIV}} – 2 ordered in 2002 from Angola and delivered in 2002 (the vehicles were previously in Angolan service). 1 ordered in 2003 from Ukraine and delivered in 2003 (the vehicle probably was previously in Ukrainian service).<ref name="SIPRI" /> 10 BMP-1 and BMP-2 in 2023, possibly non-operational{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=445}}
* {{KAZ}} – 280 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=178−179}}
[[File:Kuwaiti soldiers and a Kuwaiti BMP-2.JPEG|thumb|Kuwaiti soldiers sit beside a Kuwaiti BMP-2 infantry fighting vehicle during Operation Desert Storm.]]
* {{KUW}} – 245 along with 2,450 9M111 Fagot ATGMs were ordered in 1988 from the Soviet Union and delivered between 1989 and 1990.<ref name="Pancerni.net 1" /> Some captured or destroyed by the Iraqi forces. 46 along with 460 9M111 Fagot ATGMs were ordered in 1994 from Russia and delivered between 1994 and 1995.<ref name="SIPRI" /> 76 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=336}}
* {{KGZ}} – 90 as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=180−181}}
* {{LBY}} – Unknown number in service with the [[Government of National Unity (Libya)|Government of National Unity]]{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=87−88}}
* {{MDV}} – 2 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=273}}
* {{MKD}} – 11 were ordered in 2001 from Ukraine and delivered in 2001 (the vehicles were previously in Soviet and later Ukrainian service).<ref name="SIPRI" /><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.vojska.net/eng/armed-forces/macedonia/equipment/armor/ |title=Macedonian Armor |website=Vojska.net |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090330195231/http://www.vojska.net/eng/armed-forces/macedonia/equipment/armor/ |archive-date=30 March 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> 10 BMP-2 and 1 BMP-2K in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=112−113}}
* [[Popular Mobilization Forces]] − Unknown number in service{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=330}}
* {{RUS}} – 550 BMP-2 and BMP-2M in service with the army, 100 in service with the Naval Infantry, 50 in service with the Airborne Forces, some in service with the National Guard. Another 2,000 BMP-1 and BMP-2 (including variants) in storage.{{sfn|The Military Balance 2026|pages=190−204}} 2,350 BMP-2 and BMP-2M in service with the army, 300 in service with the Naval Infantry, and an unknown number in service with the 1st Army Corps, 2nd Army Corps, and National Guard as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=183−197}} As of August 2, 2026, Russia has been visually confirmed to have lost at least 2,190 BMP-2s of various variants (1,729 destroyed, 46 damaged, 158 abandoned, and 257 captured)<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Janovsky |first1=Jakub |last2=Black |first2=Alexander |author3=Naalsio |author4=Aloha |author5=Dan |author6=Kemal |date=24 February 2022 |title=Attack On Europe: Documenting Russian Equipment Losses During The Russian Invasion Of Ukraine |url=https://www.oryxspioenkop.com/2022/02/attack-on-europe-documenting-equipment.html |journal=Oryx |volume= |issue= |pages= |doi= |access-date=6 February 2025}}</ref>
* {{SVK}} – 90 in service as of 2025.<ref name="IISS2022_p2613" />
* {{SRI}} – 4 were ordered in 1994 from Ukraine and delivered in 1994 (the vehicles were previously in Soviet and later Ukrainian service). 36 were ordered in 2001 from Russia and delivered in 2001.<ref name="SIPRI" /> 49 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=289}}
* {{SUD}} – 6 were ordered in 1995 from Ukraine and delivered in 1996 (the vehicles were probably previously in Soviet and later Ukrainian service). 9 were ordered in 2003 from Belarus and delivered in 2003 (the vehicles were previously in Soviet and later Belarusian service).<ref name="SIPRI" /> Unknown number in service as of 2023<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mitzer |first1=Stijn |last2=Oliemans |first2=Joost |title=From Conflict To Conflict: Sudan's Fighting Vehicles |url=https://www.oryxspioenkop.com/2023/04/from-conflict-to-conflict-sudans.html |website=Oryx |access-date=29 September 2023}}</ref>
* {{SYR}} – 400 were ordered in 1987 from the Soviet Union and were delivered between 1987 and 1988.<ref name="SIPRI" /> Unknown number in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=354−355}}
* {{TJK}} – 15 as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=198}}
* {{TOG}} – 20 ordered in 1996 from Poland and delivered in 1997.<ref name="SIPRI" /> 20 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=484}}
* {{Flagicon|Transnistria}} [[Transnistria]]<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mitzer |first1=Stijn |last2=Oliemans |first2=Joost | title=The Struggle For Relevance: Transnistria's Fighting Vehicles |url=https://www.oryxspioenkop.com/2022/11/the-struggle-for-relevance.html |website=Oryx |access-date=28 September 2023}}</ref>
* {{TKM}} – 430 BMP-2 and 4 BMP-2D as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=199}}
* {{UGA}} – 31 were ordered in 2003 from Ukraine and were delivered between 2004 and 2005 (the vehicles were previously in Soviet and later Ukrainian service).<ref name="SIPRI" /> 37 as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=485}}

[[File:BMP-2 parade ukraine.jpg|thumb|Ukrainian BMP-2s on parade, 24 August 2008]]
* {{UKR}} – 890 in service with the army and 1 in service with the National Guard prior to the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]]{{sfn|The Military Balance 2022|pages=211−214}}
* {{UZB}} – 270 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=205}}
* {{VIE}} – Around 20 along with 500 9M111 Fagot ATGMs were ordered in 1982 from the Soviet Union and were delivered between 1982 and 1984.<ref name="SIPRI" /> 300 BMP-1 and BMP-2 in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=298−299}}
* {{YEM}} – 100 were ordered in 2002 from Ukraine and were delivered between 2003 and 2004 (the vehicles were probably previously in Soviet and later Ukrainian service). Between 180 and 188 BMP-2Ds were ordered in 2004 from Russia and were delivered between 2004 and 2005.<ref name="SIPRI" /> Unknown number in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=362}}
** {{flag|Houthis}} − Unknown number in service as of 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=362}}

=== Former operators ===
[[File:BMP-2 NVA.JPG|thumb|right|Ex-East German BMP-2]]
* {{AFG}} – 150 along with 1,500 9M111 Fagot ATGMs were ordered in 1987 from the Soviet Union and delivered between 1987 and 1991 (some of the vehicles were possibly previously in Soviet service).<ref name="Pancerni.net 1" /><ref name="SIPRI">{{cite web |url=http://armstrade.sipri.org/arms_trade/trade_register.php |title=SIPRI Arms Transfers Database |website=armstrade.sipri.org |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090805014045/http://armstrade.sipri.org/arms_trade/trade_register.php |archive-date=5 August 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> 550 BMP-1s and BMP-2s in service in 1992.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.istorya.ru/referat/7477/1.php |title=История России. Всемирная, мировая история – Афганистан в конце XX в |trans-title=History of Russia. Universal, World History – Afghanistan at the end of the 20th Century |language=ru |website=Istorya.ru |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090514030444/http://www.istorya.ru/referat/7477/1.php |archive-date=14 May 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Between 60 and 80 BMP-1s and BMP-2s were delivered from Russia after 2002.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.defense-ua.com/rus/news/?id=5072&prn=yes |title=Россия И Афганистан Выполняют Договоренности, Заключенные Между Военными Ведомствами Двух Странь В Кабуле В 2002 Г |trans-title=Russia and Afghanistan Fulfill Agreements Concluded Between the Military Departments of the Two Countries in Kabul in 2002 |language=ru |website=Defense-ua.com |date=29 January 2003 |access-date=20 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607174701/http://www.defense-ua.com/rus/news/?id=5072&prn=yes |archive-date=7 June 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
* {{flag|Artsakh}} − In February 2023, it was estimated to have 100 BMP-2s.{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=174}} Seized by Azerbaijan after the [[2023 Nagorno-Karabakh clashes]]<ref>{{cite news |title=Armenian separatists start surrendering weapons in Karabakh |url=https://mil.in.ua/en/news/armenian-separatists-start-surrendering-weapons-in-karabakh/ |access-date=28 September 2023 |work=Militarnyi}}</ref>
* {{CZS}} – 279 ordered in 1978 and produced between 1983 and 1989.<ref name="SIPRI" /> Passed on to the successor states.
* {{DDR}} – 24 were ordered in 1985 from the Soviet Union and were delivered between 1986 and 1987 (the vehicles were possibly produced in Czechoslovakia).<ref name="SIPRI" /> Passed on to the unified German state.
* {{GER}} – 24, taken from [[Nationale Volksarmee|East Germany's army]], all sold to other countries or given to the museums.
* {{flag|Iraq|1963}} – 200 were ordered in 1986 from the Soviet Union and were delivered between 1987 and 1989<ref name="Pancerni.net 1" />(some of the vehicles were possibly produced in Czechoslovakia).<ref name="SIPRI" /> 1,000 BMP-1 and BMP-2 in service in 1989,{{sfn|International Institute for Strategic Studies|1989|page=101}} and 900 BMP-1 and BMP-2 in 2001.<ref>{{cite book |last1=International Institute for Strategic Studies |title=The Military Balance 2001–2002 |date=2001 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-850979-0 |page=134 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WIIHAAAACAAJ |language=en |author1-link=International Institute for Strategic Studies }}</ref> Possibly captured some from Kuwait in the [[Gulf War|First Persian Gulf War]]. All destroyed in the [[2003 invasion of Iraq]] and later scrapped.
* {{JOR}} – 37 BMP-2 ordered from the Soviet Union in 1986 and delivered in 1987.<ref name="SIPRI" /> None remain in service in 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=334}}
* {{MYA}} – Unknown number of BMP-2 received from Ukraine and Russia.{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|page=199}}
* {{POL}} – 62 BMP-2s and BMP-2Ds (all of which were designed as BWP-2) ordered in 1988 and delivered in 1989. All 62 vehicles were sold to Angola in 1994. Only 42 were shipped. The remaining 20 were sold to Togo.<ref name="Pancerni.net 1" /><ref name="SIPRI" />
* {{SLE}} – 4 were ordered and delivered from Russia in 1992 (the vehicles were second-hand).<ref name="SIPRI" /> None remain in service in 2023{{sfn|The Military Balance 2023|pages=474−475}}
* {{USSR}} – 26,000 BMP-1s and BMP-2s in service in 1989.{{sfn|International Institute for Strategic Studies|1989|page=34}} Passed on to successor states.
